survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 language teacher questionnaire items (OECD, 2017) and analyzes a teacher-level analytic sample drawn from teachers who took the language teachers’ test. The manuscript does not report whether PISA complex survey weights were applied (e.g., student/teacher sampling weights) nor whether replicate weights were used, so weight usage cannot be confirmed from the provided text. Because the analysis is based on PISA questionnaire data and multigroup/SEM procedures, analysts should use the appropriate PISA teacher sampling weights from the international database when available to obtain population-representative estimates and correct standard errors under the complex design. If weights were omitted, this would limit generalizability and may affect uncertainty estimates, especially given the multigroup comparisons across countries.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in this study are teacher-reported Likert/ordinal questionnaire indicators and composite scales (e.g., teaching media literacy and metacognitive strategy dimensions), not cognitive achievement scores with PISA Plausible Values. Therefore, PV handling is not applicable because the outcomes are not PV-based achievement measures. The manuscript also does not describe any missing-data strategy (e.g., listwise deletion or imputation), which represents a reporting gap for how incomplete questionnaire responses were treated.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample consists of 20,205 language teachers who participated in the PISA 2018 tests and, for case selection, only those teachers who took the language teachers’ test. Only responses from these teachers were used because they answered specific questionnaires covering learning support, metacognitive use for learning, and metacognitive use in reading comprehension. The analysis includes teachers from selected countries/regions: Spain, Portugal, Germany, the United States, the United Kingdom, Chinese Taipei, Hong Kong, Korea, Macau, Brazil, Chile, the Dominican Republic, and Peru. The manuscript does not specify additional exclusions (e.g., missing-item rules) beyond the described selection procedure.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Teacher Questionnaire (Language teachers) — teaching media literacy (TC155Q06HA, TC155Q07HA, TC166QHA) and metacognition dimensions
main_findings.target_variable: Teaching media literacy / good Internet use (latent construct teach_prof)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM/WLSMV fit: RMSEA=0.076; TLI=0.951; CFI=0.958. Structural regression effects on teach_prof: meta_reading beta=0.540 (p=0.000); lea_supp beta=0.187 (p=0.000); meta_learning beta=-0.055 (not significant; p=0.000 reported). Model R²=0.415 (41.5% explained variance).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 teacher questionnaire the study leveraged metacognitive use in reading comprehension, learning support, and metacognitive use for learning to predict teaching media literacy/good Internet use, finding that metacognitive use in reading comprehension had the strongest positive effect (beta=0.540), learning support also had a significant positive effect (beta=0.187), and metacognitive use for learning showed no significant direct effect (beta=-0.055). This indicates that teacher training should prioritize metacognitive reading-comprehension strategies and learning-support practices to strengthen teachers’ capacity to teach students appropriate Internet use, while recognizing that the study is cross-sectional and based on self-reported questionnaire measures rather than causal evidence.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2018 language teacher questionnaire data (20,205 teachers) from selected countries/regions (Spain, Portugal, Germany, United States, United Kingdom, Chinese Taipei, Hong Kong, Korea, Macau, Brazil, Chile, Dominican Republic, Peru) to test an explanatory structural model linking teachers’ metacognitive strategy use to teaching good Internet use. The authors validate the measurement model with confirmatory factor analysis using polychoric correlations and WLSMV for ordinal items, reporting RMSEA=0.076, TLI=0.951, and CFI=0.958. In the structural regression, metacognitive use in reading comprehension is the best predictor of teaching media literacy (beta=0.540, p=0.000), learning support is also significant (beta=0.187, p=0.000), while metacognitive use for learning shows no significant direct effect (beta=-0.055). The model explains 41.5% of the variance (R²=0.415). Limitations include the absence of a documented missing-data strategy and the cross-sectional, self-report nature of the constructs, so causal claims are not warranted.
